newsitem.title: USA: US SEC eyes company forecast disclosures.
newsitem.headline: US SEC eyes company forecast disclosures.

text.p: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt said Thursday the agency has been examining the content of forward-looking corporate disclosures and has found the area "ripe for improvement."

In remarks prepared for delivery in San Diego before the Securities Regulation Institute, and released in Washington, Levitt said the agency has found little improvement in disclosure practices despite a 1995 provision protecting companies from lawsuits if forecasts do not materialize.
"Companies are using even more boilerplate," despite the requirement for "meaningful" cautionary language, Levitt said.
While analysts typically get detailed company forecasts during telephone conference calls with senior management, other investors rely largely on official disclosures required by regulators.
The so-called "safe harbor" protection against investor lawsuits was supposed to change that. But, in his speech, Levitt complained that company lawyers have gotten in the way.

Instead of taking advantage of the "safe harbor" to spell out forecasts more clearly, companies are using it to list a whole range of possible factors that might cause actual results to vary from forecasts.

"Let me just say that it is not 'meaningful' to provide only a generic laundry list of possible risks," Levitt said. "Your board (of directors) wouldn't want a boilerplate list of risks. Investors don't want it either."
In the speech, Levitt also advocated providing investors with easy-to-read information about a company before they commit to buying securities.
He also expressed interest in a proposal that would broaden the field of "material events" that require disclosure with the SEC.
"It's a safe bet that investors want to know about such events as the registration or termination of top executives, or default by the company on its corporate debt," he said.

Levitt also said he supports shortening the "quiet period" surrounding the registration of securities to a specified brief time before a filing so that it "does not chill company communication in the ordinary course of business."
Levitt set no timetable for any of the changes but listed them among "areas of improvement in the offering process that are within our grasp today."
